claim: Mormyrid fishes that can detect subtle variations in electric communication signals encode signal waveform into spike-timing differences between sensory receptors.
source: Mormyrid fishes that can detect subtle variations in electric communication signals encode signal waveform into spike-timing differences between sensory receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in the manuscript showing spike-timing differences in spiking receptors (Figure 3A,B,D) and references to previous work.

claim: The receptors of species insensitive to waveform variation produce spontaneously oscillating potentials.
source: In contrast, the receptors of species insensitive to waveform variation produce spontaneously oscillating potentials.
evidence: This claim is supported by extracellular recordings showing oscillating potentials in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Oscillating receptors respond to electric pulses by resetting their phase, resulting in transient synchrony among receptors.
source: We found that oscillating receptors respond to electric pulses by resetting their phase, resulting in transient synchrony among receptors that encodes signal timing and location, but not waveform.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing phase resets in oscillating receptors (Figure 3E,F) and transient synchrony (Figure 6).

claim: Oscillating receptors encode signal timing and location, but not waveform.
source: We found that oscillating receptors respond to electric pulses by resetting their phase, resulting in transient synchrony among receptors that encodes signal timing and location, but not waveform.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that oscillation-timing differences do not accurately encode pulse durations (Figure 3H) and that phase differences are constant regardless of pulse duration (Figure 3L).

claim: Oscillating receptors were most sensitive to frequencies found only in the collective signals of groups of conspecifics.
source: These receptors were most sensitive to frequencies found only in the collective signals of groups of conspecifics, and this was correlated with increased behavioral responses to these frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that oscillating receptors respond most strongly to 0.5-ms IPIs (Figure 7C,D), which are found only in group signals (Figure 8E,F).

claim: Increased sensitivity of oscillating receptors to group signal frequencies was correlated with increased behavioral responses to these frequencies.
source: These receptors were most sensitive to frequencies found only in the collective signals of groups of conspecifics, and this was correlated with increased behavioral responses to these frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data showing that P. tenuicauda produced the strongest EOD rate increases at the shortest IPIs tested (Figure 9C).

claim: Different perceptual capabilities correspond to different receptor physiologies.
source: Thus, different perceptual capabilities correspond to different receptor physiologies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison of spiking receptors in waveform-sensitive species versus oscillating receptors in waveform-insensitive species.

claim: Divergent sensory coding mechanisms represent adaptations for different social environments.
source: We hypothesize that these divergent mechanisms represent adaptations for different social environments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between receptor physiology and social behavior patterns described in the manuscript.

claim: This study provides the first evidence for sensory coding through oscillatory synchrony.
source: Our findings provide the first evidence for sensory coding through oscillatory synchrony.
evidence: This claim is supported by the novel data presented showing phase resets and transient synchrony in oscillating receptors.

claim: Anatomical modifications of sensory receptors and the associated brain pathway resulted in a newfound ability to detect subtle variations in electric communication signals.
source: Anatomical modifications of sensory receptors and the associated brain pathway that processes electric communication signals resulted in a newfound ability to detect subtle variations in these signals.
evidence: This claim references previous work (Carlson et al., 2011) and is supported by citation.

claim: Perceptual expansion led to a dramatic increase in the rates of signal evolution and species diversification.
source: This perceptual expansion led to a dramatic increase in the rates of signal evolution and species diversification.
evidence: This claim references previous work and is supported by citation.

claim: Mormyrid fish communicate by producing a species-specific electric organ discharge (EOD) at variable interpulse intervals (IPIs).
source: Mormyrid fish communicate by producing a species-specific electric organ discharge (EOD) at variable interpulse intervals (IPIs) (see Carlson, 2002 for review).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: The ability of some species to detect subtle variation in EOD waveforms is related to differences in the anatomy and physiology of peripheral sensory receptors called knollenorgans.
source: The ability of some species to detect subtle variation in EOD waveforms is related to differences in the anatomy and physiology of peripheral sensory receptors called knollenorgans (Harder, 1968a, 1968b; Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In species sensitive to waveform variation, knollenorgan receptors are broadly distributed across the head, back, and underbelly.
source: In species sensitive to waveform variation, these receptors are broadly distributed across the head, back, and underbelly (Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Knollenorgan receptors fire a single, time-locked spike in response to an electric stimulus in all species previously studied.
source: These receptors fire a single, time-locked spike in response to an electric stimulus in all species previously studied (Bennett, 1965; Harder, 1968b; Hopkins and Bass, 1981; Lyons-Warren et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spiking receptors encode electric pulse duration into spike-timing differences, with some receptors responding to pulse onset and others to pulse offset.
source: Spiking receptors encode electric pulse duration into spike-timing differences, with some receptors responding to pulse onset and others to pulse offset (Hopkins and Bass, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and data in Figure 3A,B,D.

claim: Spike-timing differences are compared in the midbrain.
source: These timing differences are compared in the midbrain (Friedman and Hopkins, 1998; Lyons-Warren et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Species insensitive to waveform variation have receptors that produce spontaneously oscillating potentials at frequencies up to 3 kHz.
source: In contrast, species insensitive to waveform variation have receptors that produce spontaneously oscillating potentials at frequencies up to 3 kHz (Harder, 1968b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and data in Figure 1D.

claim: Oscillating receptors are clustered into three groups, called rosettes, on each side of the head.
source: These receptors are clustered into three groups, called rosettes, on each side of the head (Harder, 1968b; Lavoue et al., 2004, 2010; Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Oscillations in neural activity are widespread throughout the brains of many animals, including humans.
source: Oscillations in neural activity are widespread throughout the brains of many animals, including humans, and are known to play important roles in generating rhythmic motor behaviors (Ramirez et al., 2004; McCrea and Rybak, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: How oscillations contribute to processes such as sleep, attention, memory, motor output, and sensory coding remains unclear.
source: However, how oscillations contribute to processes such as sleep, attention, memory, motor output, and sensory coding remains unclear (Buzsaki and Draguhn, 2004; Thut et al., 2012; Canavier, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Oscillations could facilitate multiplexed signal coding in which spikes carry information depending on the phase of the oscillation during which they occur.
source: Oscillations could facilitate multiplexed signal coding in which spikes carry information depending on the phase of the oscillation during which they occur (Thut et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothetical function of oscillations cited from previous work.

claim: Oscillations could enhance communication between neural populations during periods of synchronized excitability.
source: Another effect of oscillations could be to enhance communication between neural populations during periods of synchronized excitability (Thut et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothetical function of oscillations cited from previous work.

claim: A clear functional role for electrical oscillations in sensory processing has remained elusive.
source: Additional hypothesized functions include signal gating, feature binding, and cross-modal integration (Thut et al., 2012), although a clear functional role for electrical oscillations in sensory processing has remained elusive (Canavier, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: This is the first demonstration of information coding by oscillatory synchrony at the periphery.
source: This is the first demonstration of information coding by oscillatory synchrony at the periphery.
evidence: This claim is supported by the novel data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Phase resets in oscillating receptors did not encode pulse waveform.
source: These phase resets did not encode pulse waveform, explaining why species with oscillating receptors cannot behaviorally discriminate EOD waveform variation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing that oscillation-timing differences do not accurately encode pulse durations (Figure 3H).

claim: Species with oscillating receptors cannot behaviorally discriminate EOD waveform variation.
source: These phase resets did not encode pulse waveform, explaining why species with oscillating receptors cannot behaviorally discriminate EOD waveform variation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Carlson et al., 2011) and the physiological data showing lack of waveform encoding.

claim: Oscillating receptors may be specialized for group signal detection.
source: Furthermore, we provide physiological and behavioral evidence that oscillating receptors respond most strongly to communication signals with fast temporal patterns that are only produced by large groups of conspecifics, suggesting that oscillating receptors may be specialized for group signal detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by physiological data (Figure 7, Figure 8F) and behavioral data (Figure 9C).

claim: P. microphthalmus is behaviorally sensitive to EOD waveform variation.
source: P. microphthalmus is behaviorally sensitive to EOD waveform variation, but it evolved this ability independently of other species with broadly distributed receptors (Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: P. microphthalmus evolved the ability to detect EOD waveform variation independently of other species with broadly distributed receptors.
source: P. microphthalmus is behaviorally sensitive to EOD waveform variation, but it evolved this ability independently of other species with broadly distributed receptors (Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The receptors of P. microphthalmus fire spikes.
source: We found that the receptors of P. microphthalmus indeed fire spikes (Figure 1A), just like other mormyrids with broadly distributed receptors and EOD waveform sensitivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Spontaneous interspike intervals varied across species with spiking receptors.
source: Spontaneous interspike intervals and spontaneous oscillation periods varied across species (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spontaneous oscillation periods varied across species with oscillating receptors.
source: Spontaneous interspike intervals and spontaneous oscillation periods varied across species (Figure 1B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In P. tenuicauda, 71% of receptors had oscillation amplitudes at least 2.5 times baseline noise.
source: In P. tenuicauda, the amplitude of oscillatory activity varied from 0.04 to 6.1 mV. We only measured the frequency of spontaneous activity if the oscillation amplitude was at least 2.5 times baseline noise (≥0.1 mV). 49 of 69 (71%) receptors met these criteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from recordings in P. tenuicauda.

claim: Spontaneous oscillation amplitude was largest in the center of the rosette and progressively decreased towards the periphery.
source: Spontaneous oscillation amplitude was largest in the center of the rosette and progressively decreased towards the periphery.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Oscillation frequency and amplitude were not significantly correlated in P. tenuicauda receptors.
source: Oscillation frequency and amplitude were not significantly correlated (Spearman R = 0.27, t(22) = 1.3, p = 0.21), although frequencies tended to be highest near the center of the rosette (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from P. tenuicauda receptors.

claim: Oscillatory phase was independent across receptors in different rosettes.
source: Therefore, oscillatory phase was independent across receptors in different rosettes.
evidence: This claim is supported by circular correlation analysis showing no significant difference between simultaneous and non-simultaneous recordings (Wilcoxon matched-pairs test results reported in text).

claim: Receptors within rosettes oscillate at different frequencies.
source: Therefore, in agreement with a previous report (Harder, 1968b), oscillatory activity of individual receptors is not correlated within or across rosettes.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing beats in differential recordings (Figure 2G,H) and citation to previous work.

claim: Spiking receptors responded with a single time-locked spike in response to inward current transients.
source: As shown previously, spiking receptors responded with a single time-locked spike in response to inward current transients (Bennett, 1965), which occur at the onset of a positive-polarity pulse and at the offset of a negative-polarity pulse (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work and data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: Spike probability in spiking receptors depended on pulse duration.
source: Spike probability depended on pulse duration (Figure 3C) but was high for stimulus durations within the range of total durations of conspecific EODs (horizontal bars in Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Spike probability in spiking receptors was high for stimulus durations within the range of total durations of conspecific EODs.
source: Spike probability depended on pulse duration (Figure 3C) but was high for stimulus durations within the range of total durations of conspecific EODs (horizontal bars in Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Oscillating receptors responded to square pulses with phase resets and amplitude increases.
source: Oscillating receptors responded to square pulses with phase resets and amplitude increases (Figure 3E,F), which occurred both in receptors with high-amplitude spontaneous oscillations as well as in receptors with little to no spontaneous oscillatory activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The degree of amplitude enhancement in oscillating receptors depended on pulse duration.
source: The degree of amplitude enhancement relative to prestimulus amplitudes depended on pulse duration (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There was a positive correlation between spontaneous and stimulus-evoked oscillation amplitudes in oscillating receptors.
source: At the stimulus duration that elicited the maximum oscillation amplitude in each receptor, there was a positive correlation between spontaneous and stimulus-evoked oscillation amplitudes (Spearman R = 0.90, t(3) = 3.6, p = 0.037).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of data from oscillating receptors.

claim: Spike-timing differences in spiking receptors perfectly matched pulse duration for pulses longer than ~0.1 ms.
source: Across all spiking receptors, this spike-timing difference perfectly matched pulse duration for pulses longer than ∼0.1 ms (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Spike-timing differences accurately represented pulse duration over the behaviorally relevant ranges for total EOD duration in each species.
source: Importantly, spike-timing differences accurately represented pulse duration over the behaviorally relevant ranges for total EOD duration in each species (horizontal bars in Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Precise coding of stimulus-timing cues mediates the ability of species with spiking receptors to detect EOD waveform variation.
source: Such precise coding of stimulus-timing cues mediates the demonstrated ability of species with spiking receptors to detect EOD waveform variation (Hopkins and Bass, 1981; Arnegard et al., 2006; Machnik and Kramer, 2008; Feulner et al., 2009; Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In oscillatory receptors, positive- and negative-polarity square pulses elicited phase resets that differed by ~180°.
source: In oscillatory receptors, positive- and negative-polarity square pulses elicited phase resets that differed by ∼180° (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: The phase difference in oscillatory receptors was constant regardless of pulse duration.
source: This phase difference was constant regardless of pulse duration (Figure 3L).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Oscillation-timing differences in oscillatory receptors did not accurately encode pulse durations shorter than ~1 ms.
source: Oscillation-timing differences did not accurately encode pulse durations shorter than ∼1 ms (Figure 3H), reflecting phase resets to the leading edge of the pulse that differ by ∼180° regardless of pulse duration (Figure 3E,F,L).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Oscillatory responses could not encode pulse durations found in conspecific EODs.
source: This means that oscillatory responses could not encode pulse durations found in conspecific EODs (black bar in Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Species with oscillating receptors cannot behaviorally detect waveform variation at least in part because the precise timing cues are not encoded at the periphery.
source: Therefore, species with oscillating receptors cannot behaviorally detect waveform variation at least in part because the precise timing cues are not encoded at the periphery.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the physiological data showing lack of waveform encoding and previous behavioral data.

claim: Oscillating receptors would be able to encode the location of the stimulus based on which receptors reset to a peak first.
source: However, oscillating receptors would be able to encode the location of the stimulus based on which receptors reset to a peak first, owing to differences in stimulus polarity.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the phase reset data.

claim: At intensities for which the phase resets evoked by opposite polarity EODs were significantly different, phase differences were always ~180°.
source: At intensities for which the phase resets evoked by opposite polarity EODs were significantly different, phase differences were always ∼180° (filled circles in Figure 3K).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Spiking receptors have been reported to be most sensitive to the frequencies occurring in conspecific EOD waveforms.
source: Spiking receptors have been reported to be most sensitive to the frequencies occurring in conspecific EOD waveforms (Hopkins, 1981; Bass and Hopkins, 1984; Lyons-Warren et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The best frequencies of spiking receptors were within one octave of the peak power frequencies of conspecific EODs.
source: On average, the best frequencies of spiking receptors were within one octave of the peak power frequencies of conspecific EODs (filled symbols in Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Oscillating receptors were most sensitive to frequencies well below the peak power frequency in conspecific EODs.
source: Oscillating receptors were most sensitive to frequencies well below the peak power frequency in conspecific EODs (compare Figure 4E with black trace in Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4C.

claim: The best frequencies of oscillating receptors were more than two octaves below the peak power frequencies of conspecific EODs.
source: On average, the best frequencies of oscillating receptors were more than two octaves below the peak power frequencies of conspecific EODs (open symbols in Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The best frequencies of oscillating receptors roughly corresponded to their intrinsic oscillation frequencies.
source: At the stimulus intensity where tuning was sharpest (10 nA), the best frequencies (0.8–2.5 kHz) of oscillating receptors roughly corresponded to their intrinsic oscillation frequencies (1.5–2.0 kHz), suggesting that their frequency tuning resulted from resonance with their spontaneous oscillations.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of data on best frequencies and intrinsic oscillation frequencies.

claim: Oscillatory phase-locking was strongest for stimulus durations matching each receptor's spontaneous oscillation period.
source: Oscillatory phase-locking was strongest for stimulus durations matching each receptor's spontaneous oscillation period (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The probability that a spiking receptor fired a spike in response to both pulses in a pair decreased at the shortest intervals tested.
source: The probability that a receptor fired a spike in response to both pulses in the pair decreased at the shortest intervals tested (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Spiking receptors of all species reliably fired spikes at the reported minimum IPIs produced by individual fish (~8 ms).
source: However, receptors of all species reliably fired spikes at the reported minimum IPIs produced by individual fish (∼8 ms) (Hopkins, 1986; Carlson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5C and citations to previous work.

claim: Spiking receptors encoded IPIs into interspike intervals within receptors, with the interspike intervals exactly matching the IPI.
source: In agreement with previous studies (Bell and Grant, 1989; Baker et al., 2013), spiking receptors encoded IPIs into interspike intervals within receptors, with the interspike intervals exactly matching the IPI (Figure 5A,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5A,D and citations to previous work.

claim: Spiking receptors can faithfully encode the IPIs generated by individual signaling fish into interspike intervals within receptors.
source: Spiking receptors can therefore faithfully encode the IPIs generated by individual signaling fish into interspike intervals within receptors.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data showing accurate IPI encoding.

claim: Interoscillation intervals in oscillating receptors accurately represented the IPI for intervals of ~1 ms and longer.
source: Interoscillation intervals accurately represented the IPI for intervals of ∼1 ms and longer (Figure 5E,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5E,G.

claim: Interoscillation intervals accurately encoded IPIs over the range produced by individual fish (>8 ms).
source: Importantly, interoscillation intervals accurately encoded IPIs over the range produced by individual fish (>8 ms) (Hopkins, 1986; Carlson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5G and citations to previous work.

claim: Phase resets in oscillatory receptors serve to transiently synchronize the population in response to a stimulus.
source: Phase resets in oscillatory receptors serve to transiently synchronize the population in response to a stimulus (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Responses of oscillating receptors rapidly desynchronize because oscillation frequency varies across receptors.
source: Because oscillation frequency varies across receptors, responses rapidly desynchronize (Figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Across-receptor synchrony is greatest for the first poststimulus oscillatory peak in response to a single square pulse.
source: For instance, in response to a single square pulse, across-receptor synchrony is greatest for the first poststimulus oscillatory peak (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In response to a pair of pulses, across-receptor synchrony is high immediately following each pulse and rapidly decreases.
source: In response to a pair of pulses, across-receptor synchrony is high immediately following each pulse and rapidly decreases (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Summing responses across all 36 receptors in a rosette resulted in a single, distinct peak immediately following the stimulus.
source: Summing responses across all 36 receptors resulted in a single, distinct peak immediately following the stimulus (Figure 6D), due to a transient synchronization across receptors followed by increasing asynchrony of receptors oscillating at different frequencies.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The electrosensory system could use synchrony across the population of receptors to distinguish between stimulus-evoked and spontaneous oscillation cycles.
source: In this way, the electrosensory system could use synchrony across the population of receptors to distinguish between stimulus-evoked and spontaneous oscillation cycles.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the synchrony data.

claim: At the highest intensity tested, oscillation amplitudes in oscillating receptors were attenuated relative to single-pulse responses for IPIs below 1 ms.
source: At the highest intensity tested, oscillation amplitudes were attenuated relative to single-pulse responses for IPIs below 1 ms (black curve in Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: As stimulus intensity decreased, oscillation amplitudes in oscillating receptors became selectively enhanced in response to 0.5-ms IPIs.
source: As stimulus intensity decreased, however, oscillation amplitudes became selectively enhanced in response to 0.5-ms IPIs (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: As the intensity decreased, oscillatory responses became more sharply selective for IPIs around 0.5 ms.
source: As the intensity decreased, responses became more sharply selective for IPIs around 0.5 ms, which is near the intrinsic oscillation periods (0.47–0.99 ms) of receptors in this species.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Stimulating an oscillating receptor with a pair of pulses separated by the receptor's intrinsic oscillation period results in stronger responses.
source: This is suggestive of resonance in which stimulating an oscillating receptor with a pair of pulses separated by the receptor's intrinsic oscillation period results in stronger responses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing enhanced responses at IPIs matching intrinsic oscillation periods.

claim: At the lowest intensity tested, the phase-locking was greatest for IPIs matching receptors' intrinsic oscillation periods.
source: At the lowest intensity tested, the phase-locking was also greatest for IPIs matching receptors' intrinsic oscillation periods (light gray curve in Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Oscillating receptors produce the largest responses for IPIs matching their intrinsic oscillation periods.
source: These results reveal that oscillating receptors produce the largest responses for IPIs matching their intrinsic oscillation periods.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D,F.

claim: The intrinsic oscillation periods of oscillating receptors are at least one order of magnitude shorter than the IPIs that single fish produce.
source: These periods, however, are at least one order of magnitude shorter than the IPIs that single fish produce.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of oscillation periods (0.47-0.99 ms) with minimum IPIs produced by individual fish (~8 ms).

claim: Signals arriving at submillisecond IPIs will be easier to detect by oscillating receptors.
source: Therefore, signals arriving at submillisecond IPIs will be easier to detect, even though these IPIs are too short for each individual pulse within the train to be encoded with a phase reset.
evidence: This is an inference based on the resonance data.

claim: A large group of signaling fish may collectively produce much shorter IPIs than individual fish.
source: Even though the minimum IPI a single fish produces is approximately 8 ms, a large group of signaling fish may collectively produce much shorter IPIs.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the temporal overlap of signals from multiple fish.

claim: Group signals contained much shorter IPIs than single-fish signals.
source: Indeed, group signals contained much shorter IPIs than single-fish signals (compare Figure 8B with Figure 8A, and Figure 8E with Figure 8D; note different time scales).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The spiking receptors of P. microphthalmus could not respond to the submillisecond intervals present in collective conspecific group signals.
source: The spiking receptors of P. microphthalmus could not respond to the submillisecond intervals present in collective conspecific group signals (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Oscillating receptors responded most strongly to 0.5-ms IPIs, which are found only in group signals.
source: In contrast, oscillating receptors responded most strongly to 0.5-ms IPIs, which are found only in group signals (Figure 8F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: One advantage for species with high-frequency oscillating receptors may be the ability to detect very short IPIs in group communication signals that spiking receptors cannot encode due to refractoriness.
source: Thus, one advantage for species with high-frequency oscillating receptors may be the ability to detect very short IPIs in group communication signals that spiking receptors cannot encode due to refractoriness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of spiking and oscillating receptor responses to group signal IPIs.

claim: Species with oscillating receptors should exhibit selective behavioral responses to submillisecond IPIs.
source: If oscillating receptors facilitate detection of communication signals produced by a group of individuals, then species with oscillating receptors should exhibit selective behavioral responses to submillisecond IPIs, and species with spiking receptors should not.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by behavioral experiments.

claim: Species with spiking receptors should not exhibit selective behavioral responses to submillisecond IPIs.
source: If oscillating receptors facilitate detection of communication signals produced by a group of individuals, then species with oscillating receptors should exhibit selective behavioral responses to submillisecond IPIs, and species with spiking receptors should not.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by behavioral experiments.

claim: Mormyrids respond to electric signals by increasing or decreasing their rate of EOD production.
source: In general, mormyrids respond to electric signals by increasing or decreasing their rate of EOD production (Moller et al., 1989; Post and von der Emde, 1999; Carlson et al., 2011; Lyons-Warren et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Increases in EOD rate have been interpreted to be an orienting response to a novel stimulus.
source: Increases in EOD rate have been interpreted to be an orienting response to a novel stimulus (Post and von der Emde, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Decreases in EOD rate have been hypothesized to allow the silent fish to attend to another fish's signals or to make the silent fish electrically 'invisible' to other fish.
source: Decreases in EOD rate, or social silence, have been hypothesized to allow the silent fish to attend to another fish's signals or to make the silent fish electrically 'invisible' to other fish (Moller et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: P. tenuicauda produced the strongest EOD rate increases at the shortest and longest IPIs tested.
source: A species with oscillating receptors produced the strongest EOD rate increases at the shortest and longest IPIs tested (P. tenuicauda in Figure 9C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: The shortest IPIs (≤5 ms) correspond to those found only in signals recorded from groups of fish.
source: The shortest IPIs (≤5 ms) correspond to those found only in signals recorded from groups of fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with group signal data in Figure 8E.

claim: P. microphthalmus responded differently to IPIs than P. tenuicauda.
source: A congeneric species with spiking receptors (P. microphthalmus in Figure 9D) responded differently to IPIs than the species with oscillating receptors (repeated-measures ANOVA, interaction between species and IPI, F(6,12) = 3.4, p = 0.0048).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: P. microphthalmus produced the greatest EOD rate increases for IPIs in the intermediate range of those tested.
source: The species with spiking receptors produced the greatest EOD rate increases for IPIs in the intermediate range of those tested, which roughly correspond to the minimum IPI produced by individual fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The frequency tuning of oscillating receptors may mediate detection of submillisecond IPIs that are only present in the communication signals produced by a large group of individuals.
source: These results lend support to our hypothesis that the frequency tuning of oscillating receptors may mediate detection of submillisecond IPIs that are only present in the communication signals produced by a large group of individuals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the physiological and behavioral data.

claim: Oscillations are an adaptation for detecting large groups of conspecifics.
source: Since spiking receptors cannot encode these submillisecond IPIs, we propose that oscillations are an adapation for detecting large groups of conspecifics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the data showing enhanced sensitivity to group signal IPIs.

claim: The degree of synchrony in oscillating receptors provides information about pulse timing and polarity.
source: The degree of synchrony provides information about pulse timing and polarity, but it does not reflect the precise timing cues within the pulse waveform, consistent with the inability of these fish to behaviorally detect EOD waveform variation (Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the synchrony data and citation to previous behavioral work.

claim: Oscillating receptors are most sensitive to submillisecond IPIs that match their oscillation period (0.47–0.99 ms).
source: Further, oscillating receptors are most sensitive to submillisecond IPIs that match their oscillation period (0.47–0.99 ms).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D,F.

claim: Submillisecond IPIs are too short for spiking receptors to reliably encode.
source: This sensitivity is remarkable for two reasons. First, these submillisecond IPIs are too short for spiking receptors to reliably encode.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 8C.

claim: Submillisecond IPIs are much shorter than those produced by individual fish.
source: Second, these IPIs are much shorter than those produced by individual fish, suggesting increased sensitivity to communication signals produced by groups of individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of oscillation periods with minimum IPIs produced by individual fish.

claim: A species with oscillating receptors responded strongly to submillisecond IPIs within the range of enhanced receptor sensitivity.

claim: This novel peripheral coding mechanism may represent an adaptation for detecting communication signals from large groups of fish.
source: Thus, this novel peripheral coding mechanism may represent an adaptation for detecting communication signals from large groups of fish.

source: However, whether these phase resets encode specific information about a sensory stimulus or instead serve a modulatory function remains to be determined (Lakatos et al., 2009).

evidence: This claim is supported by data showing phase resets and transient synchrony.

claim: Sensitivity to temporal patterns has been shown to involve network interactions in a wide range of central circuits.
source: Sensitivity to temporal patterns has been shown to involve network interactions in a wide range of central circuits (Klug et al., 2012; Buonomano, 2014).

claim: Electrical oscillations in sensory receptors can act as peripheral filters for temporal patterns.
source: Here, we show that electrical oscillations in sensory receptors can act as peripheral filters for temporal patterns.

claim: Peripheral sensory receptors whose maximal sensitivity corresponds to a principal feature present in the signal they detect are considered 'matched filters'.
source: Peripheral sensory receptors whose maximal sensitivity corresponds to a principal feature present in the signal they detect are considered 'matched filters' (Wehner, 1987).

claim: Spiking receptors appear to be matched filters for conspecific EODs.

claim: The precisely timed spikes in spiking receptors enable discrimination of waveform variation.
source: Moreover, the precisely timed spikes in these receptors enable discrimination of waveform variation (Hopkins and Bass, 1981; Carlson et al., 2011), which would facilitate signaler identification.

claim: Studies on species with spiking receptors have revealed behavioral sensitivity to individual differences in conspecific EODs.
source: In fact, studies on species with spiking receptors have revealed behavioral sensitivity to individual differences in conspecific EODs (Graff and Kramer, 1992; Hanika and Kramer, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Spiking receptors are specialized for detecting communication signals produced by individual fish and encoding the information necessary to identify the sender.
source: Collectively, these results support the hypothesis that spiking receptors are specialized for detecting communication signals produced by individual fish and encoding the information necessary to identify the sender.

claim: Oscillating receptors exhibit matched filters not for EOD waveforms, but for IPI patterns in group signals.

claim: Oscillation frequencies confer enhanced sensitivity to IPIs that can only be produced by groups of fish.
source: Furthermore, these oscillation frequencies confer enhanced sensitivity to IPIs that can only be produced by groups of fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing enhanced responses to submillisecond IPIs found only in group signals.

claim: Whereas spiking receptors are specialized for detecting signals from individuals, oscillating receptors appear specialized for detecting signals from a large group.
source: Therefore, whereas spiking receptors are specialized for detecting signals from individuals, oscillating receptors appear specialized for detecting signals from a large group.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the data.

claim: The submillisecond IPIs to which oscillating receptors are most sensitive do not necessarily reflect concerted signaling amongst the group.
source: Importantly, the submillisecond IPIs to which oscillating receptors are most sensitive do not necessarily reflect concerted signaling amongst the group.

claim: Differences in receptor physiology and tuning may relate to differences in social behavior.
source: Differences in receptor physiology and tuning may relate to differences in social behavior.

claim: Species in the lineage with oscillatory receptors have been reported to school as adults and prefer open water.
source: Species in the lineage with oscillatory receptors have been reported to school as adults and prefer open water (Nichols and Griscom, 1917; Hopkins, 1980, 1981; Chapman et al., 1996; Lavoue et al., 2004; Lavoue, 2012), unlike other species, which have generally been described as solitary and territorial, and prefer areas with dense vegetation and detritus (Nichols and Griscom, 1917; Hopkins, 1980, 1981; Hopkins and Bass, 1981; Chapman et al., 1996; Friedman and Hopkins, 1996; Lavoue, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Other mormyrid species have generally been described as solitary and territorial, and prefer areas with dense vegetation and detritus.
source: Species in the lineage with oscillatory receptors have been reported to school as adults and prefer open water (Nichols and Griscom, 1917; Hopkins, 1980, 1981; Chapman et al., 1996; Lavoue et al., 2004; Lavoue, 2012), unlike other species, which have generally been described as solitary and territorial, and prefer areas with dense vegetation and detritus (Nichols and Griscom, 1917; Hopkins, 1980, 1981; Hopkins and Bass, 1981; Chapman et al., 1996; Friedman and Hopkins, 1996; Lavoue, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In single-species lab tanks, P. tenuicauda and P. soudanensis form open-water shoals and schools, respectively, while B. niger, P. adspersus, and B. brachyistius are solitary and seek shelter.
source: In single-species lab tanks, Petrocephalus tenuicauda and Petrocephalus soudanensis form open-water shoals and schools, respectively, while Brevimyrus niger, Pollimyrus adspersus, and Brienomyrus brachyistius are solitary and seek shelter (unpub. obs.).

claim: The increased sensitivity of peripheral receptors for communication signals produced by groups of conspecifics may mediate the detection and localization of shoals or schools in fish's native habitats.
source: Thus, the increased sensitivity of peripheral receptors for communication signals produced by groups of conspecifics may mediate the detection and localization of shoals or schools in fish's native habitats.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between receptor physiology and social behavior.

source: These fish, with spiking receptors and associated sensitivity to EOD waveform variation, form schools both in laboratory and natural settings (Lavoue et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

source: Indeed, damped oscillations in spike probability following an electrical stimulus in mormyrid spiking receptors may reflect subthreshold oscillations related to frequency tuning (Bennett, 1965, 1967; Roth and Szabo, 1972).

source: Spontaneous, noisy oscillations in paddlefish ampullary electroreceptors are hypothesized to contribute to prey detection (Neiman and Russell, 2001, 2011).

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

source: Furthermore, whether the oscillations that can be recorded extracellularly from rosette receptors represent collective spiking activity or non-spiking oscillatory potentials in sensory cells at the base of the receptor pore is also unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about unknown mechanisms.

source: Importantly, the oscillations in mormyrid rosette receptors are distinct from oscillations in hair cells and other electroreceptors due to their larger amplitudes and higher frequencies, as well as the fact that they respond to stimuli with phase resets.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous work and data from this study.

claim: The phase resets reported in this study are the first observed in any oscillating sensory receptor.
source: To our knowledge, the phase resets reported here are the first observed in any oscillating sensory receptor.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with previous literature.

claim: Stimulus-evoked phase resets result in transient synchrony across oscillating receptors.
source: These stimulus-evoked phase resets result in transient synchrony across oscillating receptors.

source: Since receptors have different intrinsic oscillation frequencies, this synchrony will rapidly decrease.

source: Therefore, pooling the responses of multiple receptors could mediate synchrony detection and allow for the disambiguation of stimulus-evoked and spontaneous oscillations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about central processing mechanisms.

claim: Whether and where integration of multiple receptor responses may occur remains to be determined.
source: Whether and where such integration may occur remains to be determined.
evidence: This is a statement about unknown mechanisms.

claim: A single afferent fiber could contact multiple receptors.
source: A single afferent fiber could contact multiple receptors, or multiple afferents may converge onto single postsynaptic neurons in the hindbrain nucleus of the electrosensory lateral line lobe, as reported previously in a species with spiking receptors (Bell and Grant, 1989).

claim: Multiple afferents may converge onto single postsynaptic neurons in the hindbrain nucleus of the electrosensory lateral line lobe.
source: A single afferent fiber could contact multiple receptors, or multiple afferents may converge onto single postsynaptic neurons in the hindbrain nucleus of the electrosensory lateral line lobe, as reported previously in a species with spiking receptors (Bell and Grant, 1989).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about possible integration mechanisms, with citation to previous work.

source: The entirety of our knowledge of electric communication signal coding in mormyrids had been limited to species with broadly distributed receptors (see Baker et al., 2013 for review), which fire spikes in all species that have been studied.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

source: These species' behavioral sensitivity to EOD waveform variation is due in part to the precise encoding of waveform timing cues by spiking receptors.

source: These duration-selective neurons project to the posterior exterolateral nucleus (ELp), where single-neuron selectivity for IPIs arises (Carlson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

source: Notably, species with rosette receptors have a smaller exterolateral nucleus (EL) that is not subdivided into anterior and posterior regions (Carlson et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

source: In all three species that have been studied, rosette receptors produce high-frequency oscillations (this study, Harder, 1968b).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from this study and citation to previous work.

source: When the fish emits its own EOD, receptors in all rosettes will experience stimuli of identical polarity based on the direction of current flow through the receptors (Hopkins, 1986).

source: In this case, subtracting the oscillatory responses of receptors on opposite sides of the body would result in cancellation.

source: Subtraction of these opposite-phase responses would increase oscillation amplitudes relative to single-receptor oscillations, thus potentially increasing sensitivity to external signals.

source: The mormyrid family contains two subfamilies called Mormyrinae and Petrocephalinae (Sullivan et al., 2000).
